01.note: When Rabbi Yoḥanan was chosen to head the yeshiva over Ilfa, who was away at the time, Ilfa hung himself from a ship's mast and declared that if anyone brought him a teaching from the school of Rabbi Ḥiyya and Rabbi Oshaya that he could not show was already in the Mishna, he would fall and drown. An older man came and recited a ruling about a dying man who says, give my sons a shekel each week. Ilfa answered that the ruling follows Rabbi Meir, who says it is a mitzva to carry out the instructions of the dead, and so he met the challenge.
01.why: The Gemara has just been explaining a mishna, attributed to Rabbi Meir, in which a third party must carry out a dead father's instructions; Ilfa's answer rests on that same mishna and Rabbi Meir's principle. Afterward the Gemara gives the final ruling on the sons' allowance.

people.name: Ilfa
people.about: A Sage passed over for head of the yeshiva, who stakes his life on tracing every outside teaching back to the Mishna

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: The Sage appointed head of the yeshiva instead of Ilfa

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: The Sage whose principle, that one must fulfill the instructions of the dead, Ilfa uses in his answer

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.
The foundational collection of Jewish law edited around 200 CE, which the Gemara discusses line by line.
Coins; a sela is worth two shekels.
A religious commandment or duty.

02.note: As Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi was dying, he called in his sons. He told them to honor their mother (the Gemara explains she was their stepmother), to keep his lamp lit, his table set and his bed made, and said Yosef Ḥeifani and Shimon Efrati, who served him in life, would serve him in death. After his death he came home every Shabbat eve, until a neighbor knocked and his maidservant said, Quiet, Rabbi is sitting; then he never came again. His two attendants died before him. He also summoned the Sages, told them not to eulogize him in the small towns and to reopen the yeshiva after thirty days, and named his son Shimon the Sage, his son Gamliel the Nasi, and Ḥanina bar Ḥama head of the yeshiva.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: The dying leader who gives his last instructions to his sons and to the Sages

people.name: Yosef Ḥeifani
people.about: One of the two attendants who served Rabbi in life and died before him

people.name: Shimon Efrati
people.about: The other attendant who served Rabbi in life and died before him

people.name: Gamliel
people.about: Rabbi's son, whom he names as the next Nasi; his brother Shimon is named the Sage

people.name: Ḥanina bar Ḥama
people.about: The Sage Rabbi appoints to sit at the head of the yeshiva

terms.meaning: The president or patriarch, the official leader of the Jewish community and its Sages in the Land of Israel.
The academy where the Sages studied and taught Torah.
A public speech of mourning and praise for the dead, given at funerals and memorials.

03.note: A man betrothed a woman with a mat of myrtle branches. Onlookers told him it was not worth even a peruta, the smallest coin, so he said she should be betrothed with the four dinars wrapped inside it. She took the mat and said nothing. Rava ruled that this was silence after the money had already been given, and such silence is nothing: it does not show that she accepted.
03.why: The discussion has been listing improper ways of betrothing a woman; right after this case Rava shows where his rule comes from, a baraita about a coin first handed over as a deposit, and the Gemara works out that silence there does not count as consent.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who rules on the case

terms.meaning: The first, legally binding stage of Jewish marriage, made when a man gives a woman something of value for that purpose and she accepts it.
A silver coin, worth far more than a peruta.

04.note: Rav Ḥisda kept praising Rav Hamnuna to Rav Huna as a great man, and Rav Huna asked to have him sent over. When Rav Hamnuna came, Rav Huna saw that he did not cover his head with a cloth, as Torah scholars did, and asked why. Rav Hamnuna said it was because he was not married. Rav Huna turned his face away from him and said: See that you do not see my face until you marry.
04.why: The Gemara has just discussed whether a man should study Torah first or marry first; afterward it explains that Rav Huna acted on his own view that a man still unmarried at twenty spends all his days in thoughts of sin.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: A Sage who praises Rav Hamnuna to Rav Huna

people.name: Rav Hamnuna
people.about: A promising scholar who is not yet married

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: The senior Sage who rebukes Rav Hamnuna for not marrying

05.note: Rav Dimi, arriving in Babylonia from the Land of Israel, reported that Dama ben Netina was once wearing a fine cloak of gold and sitting among the nobles of Rome. His mother came, tore the garment off him, smacked him on the head and spat in his face, and he did not embarrass her.
05.why: The Gemara is showing how far the duty to honor parents goes, using Dama ben Netina, a gentile whose honor for his father earned him a great reward; Rav Dimi adds this second report of his restraint toward his mother.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: A Sage who brings this report from the Land of Israel

people.name: Dama ben Netina
people.about: A gentile known for honoring his parents

06.note: In a Pumbedita butcher shop, a man from Neharde'a was told to wait until Rav Yehuda bar Yeḥezkel's servant was served, and mocked Rav Yehuda with an insulting name. Rav Yehuda excommunicated him and, told he often called people slaves, proclaimed him a slave. The man summoned Rav Yehuda to Rav Naḥman's court. There Rav Yehuda corrected Rav Naḥman's every word and offer, until Rav Naḥman's wife Yalta told him to get it over with. When the man claimed descent from the Hasmonean kings, Rav Yehuda quoted Shmuel that anyone who says so is a slave, and Rav Mattana, arriving that day, confirmed it. The man was proclaimed a slave and marriage contracts were torn up. When people chased Rav Yehuda to stone him, he threatened to reveal more, and they threw down their stones.
06.why: The Gemara has just taught that whoever calls others flawed is himself flawed, and Shmuel's saying that he disqualifies with his own flaw; Rav Yehuda cites that very teaching in court to justify declaring the man a slave.

people.name: Rav Yehuda bar Yeḥezkel
people.about: A Sage of Pumbedita, called Rav Yehuda, who excommunicates the man and is summoned to court

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: The judge in Neharde'a, son-in-law of the Exilarch, who hears the case

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: The Sage who advises Rav Yehuda to answer the summons

people.name: Yalta
people.about: Rav Naḥman's wife, who tells him to end the exchange

people.name: Rav Mattana
people.about: A Sage who arrives after thirteen years away and confirms Shmuel's ruling

terms.meaning: A ban imposed by the Sages that cuts a person off from normal dealings with the community until he repents.
The hereditary head of the Jewish community in Babylonia.
The Jewish royal dynasty of the Second Temple period; the story says only slaves remained of their line.
The ketubba, the document a husband gives his wife at marriage; tearing it up here marks a marriage found to be invalid.

07.note: Rav Ḥanin related that Rav Kahana once brought a bill of divorce between Sura and Neharde'a, though he did not know in which direction. Rav Kahana asked Rav whether he had to declare: It was written in my presence and it was signed in my presence. Rav said he did not have to, but that if he did, it would help. The Gemara explains: if the husband later came to contest the document, no attention would be paid to him.
07.why: The Gemara is discussing when an agent carrying a bill of divorce must make this declaration, and how Sages required it even for very short distances; this case gives Rav's ruling for travel between two towns in Babylonia.

people.name: Rav Ḥanin
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: The agent who carried the bill of divorce

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage who answers Rav Kahana's question

terms.meaning: The get, the document a husband must give his wife to end a Jewish marriage, often delivered by an agent.

terms.term: It was written in my presence and it was signed in my presence
terms.meaning: A declaration an agent bringing a bill of divorce from another place makes, so the document's validity does not need to be proved by witnesses.

08.note: A relative of Rabbi Asi held a promissory note with a property guarantee written in it, and asked Rabbi Asi whether the Sabbatical Year cancels it. Rabbi Asi said it does not. The man then went to Rabbi Yoḥanan, who said it does. Rabbi Asi came to Rabbi Yoḥanan and pointed out that Rabbi Yoḥanan himself had said it does not, and that a baraita agreed. Rabbi Yoḥanan answered: because we think so, should we act on it? Perhaps that baraita follows Beit Shammai.
08.why: The Gemara has just reported that Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish hold the Sabbatical Year does not cancel a note with a property guarantee, with baraitot in support; here Rabbi Yoḥanan refuses to rule that way in practice.

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: A Sage whose relative asks about a debt; he challenges Rabbi Yoḥanan

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Rabbi Asi's teacher, who rules that the debt is cancelled

terms.meaning: Every seventh year, when by Torah law outstanding debts are cancelled.
A clause in a loan document pledging the borrower's land as security for the debt.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.
The school of the early Sage Shammai, whose rulings are usually not followed in practice.

09.note: In Pumbedita there was a maidservant with whom people were committing forbidden sexual acts. Abaye said that were it not for Shmuel's ruling, reported by Rav Yehuda, that anyone who frees his slave violates a positive commandment, he would force her master to write her a bill of manumission. Ravina said that in a case like this, Rav Yehuda would agree she may be freed, because of the prohibition being violated.
09.why: The Gemara has been discussing when a master sends his maidservant a bill of manumission; after this case it asks whether Abaye truly rejects freeing a slave to stop a sin, citing a half-free woman whose master was forced to free her.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who would force the master to free her if not for Shmuel's ruling

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Sage who says Rav Yehuda would agree to free her here

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who reports Shmuel's ruling against freeing slaves

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who ruled that freeing one's slave violates a positive commandment

terms.meaning: A document by which a master frees a slave.
A Torah command to do something, as opposed to a prohibition.

10.note: Abba Sikkara, leader of Jerusalem's zealots and nephew of Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai, came to him in secret. Rabban Yoḥanan asked how long they would kill everyone by starvation; Abba Sikkara said the zealots would kill him if he spoke out, and told him to fake illness and death and be carried out. Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua carried him, and at the gate Abba Sikkara stopped the guards from piercing or pushing him. In the Roman camp he hailed Vespasian as king, citing verses, but fell silent at Vespasian's parable of a snake around a barrel of honey. When a messenger announced Vespasian would be emperor and his shoe would not go on, Rabban Yoḥanan explained why and how to fix it.
10.why: The Gemara is telling the story of the siege and fall of Jerusalem; just before this, the wealthy Marta bat Baitos dies in the same famine Rabban Yoḥanan blames on the zealots.

people.name: Abba Sikkara
people.about: Leader of the zealots of Jerusalem and nephew of Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai

people.name: Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai
people.about: A leading Sage who escapes the besieged city to meet the Roman commander

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: One of the students who carry him out of the city

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: The other student who carries him out

people.name: Vespasian
people.about: The Roman commander besieging Jerusalem, who is named emperor

terms.meaning: Armed rebels inside besieged Jerusalem who refused any peace with Rome.
The holy sanctuary in Jerusalem, center of Jewish worship, which the Romans destroyed.

10.flag: The STORY segments stop mid-scene: Vespasian's offer and Rabban Yoḥanan's request for Yavne, the outcome of the meeting, sit in the AFTER segments.

11.note: Onkelos bar Kalonikos, Titus's nephew, wanted to convert. He raised Titus from the dead by necromancy and asked who matters most in that world. Titus said the Jewish people, but told him their commandments were too many to keep and he should fight them instead; asked his own punishment, Titus said his ashes are gathered, judged, burned and scattered over the seven seas every day. Onkelos raised Balaam, who told him not to seek their peace, and is punished in boiling semen. Then he raised Jesus the Nazarene, who told him to seek their welfare, and is punished in boiling excrement. The Gemara draws the contrast between the sinners of Israel and the prophets of the nations. The text here does not say what Onkelos then did.
11.why: The Gemara has just told of Titus's death and his order that his ashes be scattered so the God of the Jews could not judge him; here that very sentence is carried out on him every day.

people.name: Onkelos bar Kalonikos
people.about: Titus's sister's son, who wants to convert to Judaism

people.name: Titus
people.about: The Roman who destroyed the Temple, raised from the dead by Onkelos

people.name: Balaam
people.about: The gentile prophet of the Bible who wished Israel harm, raised by Onkelos

people.name: Jesus the Nazarene
people.about: Raised by Onkelos; the Gemara calls him a sinner of Israel who sought their welfare

terms.meaning: Calling up the spirit of a dead person to speak with them.
To become Jewish by formally accepting the Torah and its commandments.

12.note: At the King's Mountain it was the custom to carry a rooster and a hen before a bride and groom. One day Roman soldiers took them, the people beat the soldiers, and the soldiers told the emperor the Jews had rebelled. He attacked. Bar Deroma, who could leap a mil, killed many Romans, until he quoted a psalm as a complaint against God; then a snake eviscerated him in an outhouse and he died. The emperor withdrew, but when the Jews celebrated with lamps, he said they were rejoicing over him and returned. Rav Asi says three hundred thousand swordsmen massacred the people for three days and nights while weddings went on at the other side, neither knowing of the other.
12.why: The Gemara is recounting disasters of the war with Rome; it said earlier that the King's Mountain was destroyed over a rooster and a hen, and after the story of Kamtza and bar Kamtza it now gives the details.

people.name: bar Deroma
people.about: A man of the King's Mountain who could leap a mil and killed many Romans

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: The Sage who reports the size of the massacre

terms.meaning: Tur Malka, a large, heavily populated region of the Land of Israel.
A unit of distance, roughly a kilometer.

13.note: When Rav Ashi wanted his slave Minyamin immersed, he handed him to Ravina and Rav Aḥa son of Rava, warning that he would hold them responsible. They put a bridle on his neck, loosened it at the moment of immersion and tightened it again at once; the Gemara explains this let the water reach him and kept him from declaring first that he was immersing to become a free man. As he lifted his head from the water they put a bucket of clay on it and told him: Go, take this to your master's house.
13.why: Shmuel has just said that to stop a slave from declaring his immersion is for freedom, the owner must hold him tightly in the water; this incident shows how that was done.

people.name: Minyamin
people.about: Rav Ashi's slave, who is to be immersed

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Minyamin's master

people.name: Ravina
people.about: One of the two Sages who carry out the immersion

people.name: Rav Aḥa son of Rava
people.about: The other Sage who carries out the immersion

terms.meaning: Dipping in a ritual pool; a slave immersed for slavery joins a Jewish household as a slave, but if he immerses for freedom it makes him a free Jew.
Anything between the body and the water, which makes a ritual immersion invalid.

14.note: When Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda came from the Land of Israel, he reported that Rabbi Zakkai once recited a baraita before Rabbi Yoḥanan: an Ammonite woman is fit, her son from an Ammonite man is unfit, and her daughter is fit, but only when both parents converted; her daughter from an Ammonite married to a Jewish woman is unfit. Rabbi Yoḥanan told him: Go out and teach it outside. He took the teaching apart line by line, showing which parts were obvious, and rejected the last line.
14.why: Rav Yosef has just supported Rabbi Yoḥanan's view that the daughter of an Ammonite convert and a Jewish woman may marry a priest; this report shows Rabbi Yoḥanan dismissing a baraita that says otherwise.

people.name: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who brings this report from the Land of Israel

people.name: Rabbi Zakkai
people.about: The Sage who recites the baraita

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: The Sage who rejects the baraita

terms.meaning: A member of a nation the Torah bars from marrying into Israel; the Sages apply the ban to men only.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

terms.term: Go out and teach it outside
terms.meaning: A dismissal: this teaching is unreliable and should not be studied in the study hall.
Families of priests descended from Aaron, who may marry only women of qualifying lineage.

15.note: The daughters-in-law of Abdan rebelled against their husbands, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi sent two Sages to look into it. When some women said to the daughters-in-law, Look, your husbands are coming, they answered: Let them be your husbands. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said: There is no greater refusal than this.
15.why: The Gemara is asking whether something other than a formal refusal can end a minor's marriage, even after full marriage; it brings this case, argues the women may only have been betrothed, and still rules with Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira.

people.name: Abdan
people.about: The man whose daughters-in-law rebel against their husbands

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: The leader of the Sages who sends two Sages and rules on the case

terms.meaning: A girl married off as a minor by her mother or brother could leave the marriage by declaring she refuses her husband, without a divorce.
Jewish marriage had two stages: betrothal, which already binds the couple, and full marriage, when they begin living together.

16.note: In a time of Roman persecution, a question had to be sent to the Sages. Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei says it concerned a girl who, as a minor, married a man's maternal uncle, and then married that man's paternal brother, who died: could she now refuse her first marriage, undoing it, so that her co-wife could marry the man in levirate marriage? Those involved hired two men for four hundred dinars, who asked Rabbi Akiva in prison and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira in Netzivin. Both forbade it.
16.why: The Gemara is identifying which Sages stand behind the mishna's rules on a minor who left one husband by divorce and another by refusal; Rav cited this episode, and Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei corrects which question was asked.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage who says what question was really asked

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage held in a Roman prison, who forbids it

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
people.about: A Sage in Netzivin, who also forbids it

terms.meaning: A girl married off as a minor could leave the marriage by declaring she refuses her husband, which undoes it.
When a man dies childless, his brother may marry his widow, or one of his widows if he had several.
Another wife of the same husband.
A relative one may not marry by rabbinic law, beyond the Torah's own list.

16.flag: The STORY segments start mid-account: the first version of the episode (the hired messenger, Rabbi Akiva in prison) is in the BEFORE segments, and segment 4 opens with Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei's correction of it.

17.note: The sons of Rabbi Ḥiyya went out to the villages, forgot what they had learned, and struggled to recall it. One asked whether their dead father knew of their anguish. The other answered from Job: His sons are honored yet he shall not know it. The first replied with the next verse, Only in his flesh does he feel pain, and Rabbi Yitzḥak's teaching that maggots hurt the dead like a needle in living flesh. They concluded that the dead know of their own pain but not of the pain of others.
17.why: The Gemara has just said the righteous are called living even in death and applied 'the dead know nothing' to the wicked; the brothers' exchange asks what the dead know, and the Gemara then challenges their answer with a story of spirits in a cemetery.

people.name: The sons of Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: Two brothers who forget their learning and wonder whether their father knows

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: Their dead father

people.name: Rabbi Yitzḥak
people.about: A Sage whose teaching about the pain of the dead one brother quotes

18.note: Shimon HaPakuli arranged the eighteen blessings in order before Rabban Gamliel in Yavne. Rabban Gamliel asked the Sages whether anyone knew how to compose the blessing against the heretics, and Shmuel HaKatan stood up and composed it. The next year, leading the prayer, he forgot it and spent two or three hours trying to recall it, and they did not remove him.
18.why: The Gemara has just asked why the prayer of eighteen blessings has nineteen, answering that the blessing of the heretics was added in Yavne; afterward it asks why Shmuel HaKatan was not removed, since a leader who errs in that blessing is suspected of heresy.

people.name: Shimon HaPakuli
people.about: The Sage who set the eighteen blessings in order

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The Nasi, head of the Sages in Yavne, who asks for the new blessing

people.name: Shmuel HaKatan
people.about: The Sage who composes the blessing against the heretics and later forgets it

terms.meaning: The central prayer of the Jewish service, recited standing, also called the Amida.
A blessing added to the prayer asking God to defeat informers and heretics.
The town where the Sages gathered and led the community after the destruction of the Temple.
The person who recites the prayer aloud on behalf of the congregation.

19.note: Ulla visited Rav Naḥman, ate, led Grace after Meals, and handed the cup of blessing to Rav Naḥman. Rav Naḥman asked him to send the cup to his wife Yalta. Ulla refused, citing Rabbi Yoḥanan that a woman's offspring are blessed only through her husband, from the verse: He will bless the fruit of your body. Yalta heard, rose in a rage, went into the wine store and broke four hundred barrels of wine. At Rav Naḥman's request Ulla sent her another cup with word that all the wine in the barrel was wine of blessing. She sent back: from peddlers, words, and from rags, lice.
19.why: The Gemara has just listed how the cup of blessing is handled, ending with sending it to one's household so one's wife will be blessed; Ulla's refusal disputes that last practice.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: A visiting Sage who leads Grace after Meals and refuses to send Yalta the cup

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: Ulla's host, Yalta's husband

people.name: Yalta
people.about: Rav Naḥman's wife, who smashes the wine barrels in anger

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: The Sage whose teaching Ulla quotes

people.name: Rabbi Natan
people.about: A Sage who taught the same idea in a baraita

terms.meaning: The blessings said after eating bread, sometimes over a cup of wine.
The cup of wine held while leading Grace after Meals, then drunk and shared.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

20.note: Rav Avya came to Rava's house with clay on his feet and put them on the bed. Rava grew angry and set out to torment him with hard questions: why may a naphtha lamp be moved on Shabbat? Rav Avya said it can be used to cover a vessel. Rava objected that then every pebble in the yard could be moved too. Rav Avya answered that a lamp has the status of a vessel and pebbles do not, citing a baraita on jewelry and Ulla's reason for it. Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak said: Thank God that Rava did not embarrass Rav Avya.
20.why: Rabba and Rav Yosef have just ruled, against Rav Yehuda, that even a naphtha lamp may be moved on Shabbat; Rava's challenge asks for their reason, and Rav Avya supplies it.

people.name: Rav Avya
people.about: A guest at Rava's house who answers his hard questions

people.name: Rava
people.about: The host, angry at the dirtied bed

people.name: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak
people.about: The Sage who gives thanks that Rav Avya was not shamed

people.name: Ulla
people.about: A Sage whose reason Rav Avya cites

terms.meaning: A lamp burning crude oil, whose bad smell means it is used only for light.
Muktze: objects that may not be moved on Shabbat because they were not meant for use that day.
Being a usable utensil, which allows an object to be moved on Shabbat more freely than raw materials like pebbles.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.
